question: What is the primary function of memory cells generated by vaccination?

options.A: To produce rapid neutralizing antibodies upon future exposure
options.C: To manufacture red blood cells in secondary lymphoid organs
options.D: To secrete inflammatory cytokines during an acute infection

explanation: Memory cells remain in the body long-term to recognize and respond swiftly if the same pathogen invades again, preventing disease. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h1)

question: Why do vaccines fail to cause full-blown clinical disease in healthy recipients?

options.A: They rely exclusively on passive immunity provided by maternal antibodies
options.B: They contain live pathogens that multiply too slowly to cause harm
options.C: They use weakened, inactivated, or partial components of the organism
options.D: They are neutralized immediately by the acidic environment of the skin

explanation: Formulations are deliberately altered or fragmented so they stimulate immunological memory while stripping away virulence factors. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h1)

question: Which vaccine category uses killed microorganisms that are incapable of replication?
explanation: Inactivated formulations use pathogens that have been killed using heat or chemicals, meaning they cannot multiply inside the host. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h2)

question: A patient asks why their toxoid vaccine requires multiple booster doses over time. What is the underlying reason?

options.A: Toxoids lack adjuvants entirely, preventing any localized inflammatory response
options.B: Toxoids are rapidly cleared by the liver before the immune system can process them
options.C: Toxoids contain live bacteria that mutate inside the muscle tissue
options.D: Toxoids target metabolic toxins rather than the organism itself, yielding shorter-lived immunity

explanation: Because toxoids neutralize bacterial poisons rather than replicating pathogens, they stimulate less durable immunologic memory, necessitating boosters. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h2)

question: At what age is the BCG vaccine routinely scheduled for administration in a Nigerian newborn?
explanation: BCG is given at birth or as early as possible thereafter to protect infants against severe forms of childhood tuberculosis. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h3)

question: Which set of vaccines is routinely introduced during the 14-week immunization visit in the Nigerian schedule?

options.A: Third doses of pentavalent, pneumococcal conjugate, and polio vaccines
options.B: BCG and birth dose of oral polio
options.D: Vitamin A supplementation and first rotavirus dose

explanation: The 14-week visit marks the completion of the primary series for several multi-dose injectable and oral infant vaccines in the schedule. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h3)

question: What is the standard acceptable temperature range for storing most routine vaccines in a clinic refrigerator?

options.A: Plus 30 degrees Celsius to plus 40 degrees Celsius
options.B: Plus 2 degrees Celsius to plus 8 degrees Celsius
options.C: Plus 15 degrees Celsius to plus 25 degrees Celsius
options.D: Minus 20 degrees Celsius to minus 10 degrees Celsius

explanation: Maintaining storage between +2°C and +8°C prevents both heat denaturation and freezing damage for the majority of routine immunizing agents. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h4)

question: A nurse is preparing to administer the routine BCG vaccine to a newborn. Which injection route and expected skin reaction should the nurse anticipate?

options.A: Subcutaneous injection into the fatty back of the arm causing localized redness
options.B: Oral drops swallowed directly into the gastrointestinal tract with no skin sign
options.C: Intradermal injection over the insertion of the left deltoid producing a pale raised bleb
options.D: Intramuscular injection into the vastus lateralis resulting in a firm nodule

explanation: BCG is given intradermally, typically on the upper left arm, creating a characteristic wheal or bleb that confirms correct placement. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h4)

question: How is an Adverse Event Following Immunization (AEFI) best defined?

options.A: Any untoward medical occurrence following vaccination regardless of direct causality
options.B: A localized bacterial infection acquired through unsterile needle reuse
options.C: A severe allergic reaction that develops within five minutes of an injection
options.D: A proven toxic reaction directly caused by faulty vaccine manufacturing

explanation: An AEFI is defined broadly to capture any health issue occurring after immunization, which then undergoes investigation to determine if it was caused by the vaccine, delivery error, or coincidence. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h5)

question: Which type of AEFI is caused by incorrect reconstitution, incorrect dosage measurement, or unsterile administration practices?
explanation: Program errors stem from mistakes in handling, storage, or administration by healthcare personnel rather than inherent properties of the vaccine itself. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h5)

question: Which condition is a permanent contraindication for administering live-attenuated vaccines?

options.A: Severe cellular immunodeficiency or active immunosuppressive therapy
options.B: Mild upper respiratory tract infection with a clear runny nose
options.C: A history of mild localized soreness after a previous tetanus shot
options.D: Low-grade fever associated with teething in an infant

explanation: Immunocompromised individuals cannot control replicating agents in live-attenuated vaccines, putting them at high risk for disseminated disease. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h6)

question: Why are pregnant women advised against receiving live-attenuated vaccines while remaining eligible for certain inactivated ones?

options.A: Live vaccines can theoretically infect the developing fetus, whereas inactivated ones cannot replicate
options.B: Inactivated vaccines pass through the placenta and cause immediate fetal distress
options.C: Pregnancy completely destroys the body's ability to produce antibodies against toxins
options.D: Maternal blood volume increases so rapidly that vaccines are washed out before absorption

explanation: Because live organisms replicate, they pose a theoretical risk of fetal infection, whereas killed or fractionated vaccines lack this risk. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h6)

question: What is the primary benefit of achieving high herd immunity within a community?

options.A: It protects vulnerable individuals who cannot be vaccinated by reducing overall transmission
options.B: It guarantees that cold chain storage failures will never affect vaccine potency
options.C: It eliminates the need for any future booster doses for adults and children
options.D: It completely eradicates all bacterial pathogens from the local water supply

explanation: When the vast majority of a population is immune, the pathogen cannot easily circulate, shielding those who are medically ineligible for vaccination. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h7)

question: How should a nurse best respond to a parent expressing deep fear and hesitancy regarding childhood vaccines due to rumors?

options.A: Dismiss the rumors as foolish and insist on immediate compliance without discussion
options.B: Refuse to provide any medical care to the child until the parent agrees
options.C: Listen empathetically, validate concerns, and provide clear, factual health education
options.D: Report the parent immediately to local health authorities for child neglect

explanation: Building trust through respectful dialogue and evidence-based education is the most effective approach to overcoming vaccine hesitancy. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T16#GNS215_U6_T16_h7)
